group: Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk
question:
Patient note:
A 69-year-old man was assessed late this afternoon in the pre-admission clinic seven days before a planned open right hepatic lobectomy for a 4.5-cm segment VIII mass suspicious for cholangiocarcinoma that was found on surveillance MRI for primary sclerosing cholangitis; the hepatobiliary team anticipates a subcostal chevron incision, intermittent Pringle maneuvers, operative time of five to six hours, anticipated blood loss of 600 – 900 mL, and transfer post-closure to the surgical intensive care unit for invasive hemodynamic monitoring. He arrived driving himself from his rural home, walked the two blocks from the parking garage briskly, and climbed one flight of stairs because a volunteer was using the elevator, stating that he felt only mild exertional thigh fatigue but no shortness of breath, chest pressure, or light-headedness. At home he remains fully independent, mows half an acre with a self-propelled mower in two sessions, and routinely carries twenty-pound bags of water-softener salt from the garage to the basement without needing to pause. He sleeps flat, has not awakened gasping, and has noted no pedal swelling or unexpected weight gain; his last transthoracic echocardiogram, obtained two months ago to document baseline cardiac function before portal-vein embolization, showed a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 60 % with normal chamber dimensions and no valvular abnormality. Nine years earlier he experienced sudden left-sided weakness and slurred speech while loading lumber; brain MRI demonstrated an acute right corona radiata infarct without hemorrhage, and computed-tomography angiography revealed no large-vessel occlusion. He received intravenous alteplase within the therapeutic window, completed three weeks of inpatient rehabilitation, and has had no recurrence—follow-up neurologic examination last month revealed full strength, intact coordination, and only trace asymmetry of the left nasolabial fold when smiling. Secondary-prevention measures include aspirin 81 mg daily, rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly, and lifestyle modification with regular exercise and a plant-forward diet. He has never required insulin or other glucose-lowering agents and reports fasting plasma glucose readings in the low 90s during annual wellness checks; hemoglobin A1c last quarter was 5.6 %. Essential hypertension, first noted in his early fifties, is well controlled on lisinopril 20 mg every morning and hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg; home logs averaged 124/72 mm Hg over the past month. He denies any history of myocardial infarction, angina, coronary revascularization, intermittent claudication, chronic lung disease, heart rhythm disturbances, or syncope. Surgical history includes uncomplicated laparoscopic appendectomy at age 27 and a right inguinal herniorrhaphy performed under local anesthesia five years ago. He quit cigarette smoking at 40 after a 15-pack-year exposure, drinks an IPA with Friday dinner, and has never used recreational drugs. Family history is notable for a brother who underwent carotid endarterectomy at 66 and a father who died of complications of cirrhosis at 78; there are no premature coronary deaths. Review of systems today is negative for fever, chills, cough, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, palpitations, abdominal pain beyond dull right upper-quadrant pressure, melena, hematochezia, urinary symptoms, or unintentional weight change—he intentionally lost seven pounds over the past two months by reducing refined carbohydrates. After five minutes of seated rest, vitals measured in the right arm were blood pressure 118/66 mm Hg, regular pulse 68 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air, and oral temperature 36.5 °C; he is 181 cm tall and weighs 84 kg, yielding a body-mass index of 25.7 kg/m². He appeared well nourished and in no distress. Jugular venous pulsation was less than 3 cm above the sternal angle with the head of the bed at 45°, carotid upstrokes were brisk without bruit, and the point of maximal impulse was located in the fifth interspace at the mid-clavicular line. Cardiac auscultation revealed a crisp S1 and S2 with no murmurs, gallops, or rubs; lungs were clear to percussion and auscultation throughout. The abdomen was soft with a palpable, mildly tender mass under the right costal margin; there was no ascites, rebound, or guarding. Extremities were warm with 2+ dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses and no edema or cyanosis. Neurologic screening demonstrated full orientation, intact cranial nerves, 5/5 strength in all extremities, normal sensation to light touch and vibration, and a steady tandem gait. Pre-operative laboratory studies drawn one hour earlier showed hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, hematocrit 41 %, white blood cells 6.4 × 10⁹/L, platelets 232 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 19 mg/dL, and a serum creatinine of 1.23 mg/dL, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of approximately 67 mL/min/1.73 m²; liver chemistries showed alanine aminotransferase 56 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 60 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 298 U/L, total bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL with direct fraction 0.6 mg/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.1. Twelve-lead electrocardiography revealed normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats/min with normal intervals and no ST-segment deviation when compared with a tracing obtained six months prior. Upright postero-anterior chest radiograph showed clear lung fields and a normal cardiomediastinal silhouette. Airway assessment documented Mallampati class I view, inter-incisor distance 4 cm, thyromental distance 7 cm, and full cervical extension. The anesthesiology plan is to continue antihypertensive, antiplatelet, and statin therapy on the morning of surgery, allow clear liquids until two hours pre-arrival, induce balanced general anesthesia with epidural catheter placement for postoperative analgesia, insert radial arterial and central venous lines, employ goal-directed fluid therapy mindful of anticipated blood loss, and monitor point-of-care coagulation parameters every two hours intraoperatively. Sequential compression devices, incentive spirometry, early ambulation, and prophylactic subcutaneous heparin beginning the evening of surgery were reviewed; after a discussion of bleeding, bile leak, liver failure, pulmonary, renal, cardiac, and neurologic risks, the patient demonstrated accurate teach-back regarding fasting instructions and postoperative expectations and wished to proceed with definitive liver resection.

Question: What is the patient's score of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index assigns 1 point for each of six preoperative criteria:
- High-risk surgery: The planned open hepatic lobectomy is intraperitoneal = 1.
- Ischemic heart disease: No history of infarction, angina, or coronary revascularization = 0.
- Heart failure: No history or clinical evidence of heart failure = 0.
- Cerebrovascular disease: The prior ischemic stroke counts despite neurologic recovery = 1.
- Preoperative insulin treatment: He does not use insulin = 0.
- Preoperative creatinine >2.0 mg/dL: His creatinine is 1.23 mg/dL = 0.
RCRI = 1 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 0 = 2.
Final answer: 2
